newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Guatemala denies striking U.N. deal with China.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala denies striking U.N. deal with China.

text.p: Guatemala denied on Tuesday it had struck a deal with China to break off diplomatic relations with Taiwan in exchange for Beijing not vetoing a United Nations mission to the Central American country.

"Absolutely and categorically Guatemala maintains full diplomatic relations with Taiwan," Foreign Minister Eduardo Stein told a news conference in Brussels. "This has never been the subject of negotiations with China."
Stein was speaking a day after the U.N. Security Council unanimously approved sending 155 military observers to monitor peace accords in Guatemala that ended three decades of civil war.
China had vetoed an earlier vote because of Guatemala's strong links to Taiwan, but relented after 10 days of intense negotiations.

Stein, in Brussels with Guatemalan President Alvaro Arzu for talks on European Union aid, said no commitments had been made, although a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman in Beijing said Guatemala had promised to support no longer Taiwan's bid to be reinstated as a U.N. member.
"They pledged to respect the provisions of Resolution 2758 of the General Assembly and to use it as a guide to relevant actions in the United Nations," the spokesman said.

Stein did not comment directly on that, but said: "There has been a positive clarifying process. There has been a situation whereby we have been able to persuade them (China) of the absurdity of the situation they were forcing us into."

For the past four years Guatemala has been among a number of small countries which have sought the inscription of a new General Assembly agenda item aimed at establishing a committee to consider U.N. membership for Taiwan. Taipei has given generous aid to these countries.
Taipei was expelled from the world body in 1971 and replaced by Beijing as the rightful representative of China.

Arzu and Stein are on a week-long European tour to promote Guatemala's plans to implement ambitious promises in a peace treaty signed on December 29 between the government and the leftist Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels.

The Guatemalan government has calculated that it needs some $2.5 billion for programmes to modernise the state, combat poverty and resettle hundreds of thousands of Guatemalans displaced during 36 years of conflict.
Under the peace agreements, the Guatemalan army is to cut its numbers and about 3,000 guerrillas from the URNG are to go to assembly points, disarm and be integrated into civilian life.
